title: Lesson 4: The OASYS Process

blocks.html:
Eleven months in. The two-day session was last spring, you've facilitated three quarterly planning days since, and the CEO opens with: “So — are we done? What happens now?”

It sounds like a scheduling question. It isn't. It's the moment a client decides whether this was a project they completed or a rhythm they're now in, and what you say in the next thirty seconds shapes year two.

This lesson gives you that answer, along with the rest of what a client experiences: the three ways owners approach this work, how success is actually measured, and what to say to a prospect who wants only the software.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to:

  1. Describe the first year and every year after it accurately, session by session.
  2. Explain the three client options and why we recommend the coached engagement — without dismissing the do-it-yourself path.
  3. Measure success the way the practice does: ten factors improving, not one finish line.

About 20 minutes, including three short videos.

blocks.html:
What changed since these videos were recorded (2026)
Each year, including year one, is one two-day annual session plus three one-day quarterlies, ongoing, with no planned end. In year one the two-day session carries the Foundation work.

Three ways owners approach it

All three are legitimate. Watch what each one gets, and where each one usually stalls.

Do it aloneGroup coachingDone for you — OASYS
What they getA book — usually Traction or Scaling Up — and their own reading of it.Some structure and other owners to compare with.Facilitated sessions, the tools set up with them, and a coach in the room watching how the team actually behaves.
Where it stallsMonth three: the team drifts back, and there's nobody outside to notice.The cadence fits the group's calendar, not the company's quarter.It doesn't — provided the owner does the work between sessions.
The honest limitWorks for a disciplined owner with a strong team.Works as a bridge for a smaller company.Needs an owner willing to be coached, not just advised.

The comparison isn't a sales device — it's the reason the recommendation is what it is. Like a coach on the sidelines, we're not better at the game than the players. We're better at watching, knowing what to look for, and helping them improve. Say that before you say anything about what we offer.

Why OneAccord always recommends the full engagement

We help set up the tools, facilitate the initial and ongoing planning sessions, and coach the leadership team. That's where clients get the most value, and it's what we lead with — every time.

For prospects who genuinely can't support a full engagement yet, we can set them up on ninety.io to self-implement and stay their go-to resource when bigger issues come up. That's a real option, offered honestly — it isn't a consolation prize, and it isn't a discount conversation. Cost and scope belong with the Managing Principal; your job is to describe the options accurately and let the right person price them.

blocks.title: Starting Strong and Maintaining Momentum: The OASYS Journey

blocks.note: Listen for: how Doug defines success, and the steps of the engagement from first assessment into the ongoing annual cadence.

blocks.html:
How success is measured

Success isn't one end goal, like selling the company. It's getting steadily better at ten things — and they map onto the three owner objectives:

The objectiveWhat improving looks like
Purpose and goalsA solid strategy · a shared vision · the right things getting done each 90 days
Time freedomThe right people in the right seats · great teamwork · consistent execution · a leadership team that solves its own issues
Enterprise valueThe right numbers (KPIs) · financial performance · enterprise value itself

This is what to say when an owner asks how they'll know it's working. Not “you'll hit the target” — “you'll be measurably better at these ten things, and you'll see it quarter by quarter.”

The engagement journey

  1. Baseline: a OneAccord business assessment, an enterprise value appraisal, and behavioural and team assessments (for example DISC, Working Genius, and Five Dysfunctions trust-building).
  2. Situation analysis and proposal, then agreement with the owner or CEO.
  3. Two-day onboarding in year one: day one is Foundation Setting — values, purpose, the one-page plan, the scorecard and the meeting rhythm. Day two is Vision and Goal Setting — the long-term vision and the goals that follow from it. Coaches may adapt how they run the two days; the work they carry is fixed.
  4. Weekly meetings: we coach the leadership team's first weekly meetings, then the agenda rolls out through the company.
  5. Quarterly planning: dates set for a rolling 12 months; we facilitate each 90-day session, ideally in person.
  6. Every year after that: one two-day annual session plus three one-day quarterly sessions — ongoing, with no planned end. From year two the annual session focuses on long-term vision and the next 90-day plan.
  7. Graduation: a client may graduate once they can sustain the cadence themselves. It's allowed, and it isn't the design goal.

So the answer to “are we done?” at the end of year one is: no — this is the rhythm now. Year one built the foundation; from here it's an annual session and three quarterlies, every year, with the plan refreshed each quarter.

blocks.prompt: A prospect asks what year two looks like. What's the accurate answer?
options: Nothing — the implementation workshops finish and they're done
One two-day annual session plus three one-day quarterly sessions, ongoing, with no planned end
Monthly coaching calls for as long as they want them
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Year one is the two-day onboarding (Foundation Setting, then Vision and Goal Setting) plus three quarterlies; every year after is a two-day annual plus three quarterlies, continuing.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Each year, including year one, is one two-day session plus three one-day quarterlies, ongoing with no planned end. The older “three implementation workshops and you're done” framing is out of date.

blocks.prompt: What does year one's two-day session carry?
options: Sales training and a budget review
Day one Foundation Setting, day two Vision and Goal Setting
A SWOT analysis and a hiring plan
A software setup day and a demo
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct — and coaches may adapt how they run the two days, but that's the work they carry.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Day one is Foundation Setting, day two is Vision and Goal Setting. That's the Foundation work, and it's why year one's annual session is the two-day onboarding.

blocks.prompt: Which option does OneAccord always recommend?
options: Do it yourself after reading Traction
The full coached OASYS engagement with an implementer coach
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Lead with the full coached engagement; self-implementation on ninety.io is an honest fallback for clients who can't support a full engagement yet.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: We always recommend the full coached engagement. Self-implementation is a real option for budget-limited clients, not the recommendation.

blocks.prompt: How does the practice define success in an engagement?
options: Steady improvement across ten factors that serve the owner objectives
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Exactly. Ten factors, improving quarter by quarter — continuous improvement, not one finish line.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Success is steady improvement across ten factors, from strategy and vision to financial performance and enterprise value — all of them serving the three owner objectives.

blocks.promptHtml:
Final exercise: explain OASYS in about a minute.

A CPA you work with introduces you to one of her clients, the owner of a growing manufacturing company: "He's stretched thin, his team isn't aligned, and he says he'd like to sell in five or six years. I told him you might be able to help."

Write what you'd say to the owner, in about 150 to 250 words, the way you'd actually say it.
rubric: Connects to his situation and at least one owner objective (time freedom, alignment on goals, or enterprise value and exit readiness)
Explains what OASYS does: a strategic plan plus an upgraded operating system, run on ninety.io, so the plan actually gets executed

Describes how an engagement works at a high level (assessment, implementation workshops, 90-day planning cadence, annual retreat, and ongoing coaching year after year, with graduation allowed but not the goal)
Explains why the coached approach beats doing it alone, without dismissing the DIY option
Proposes a clear, low-pressure next step and does not quote prices
blocks.coachContext: OneAccord's OASYS Strategic Planning practice (older materials and videos call it SPE, Strategic Planning and Execution; Doug sometimes says 'Oasis') helps clients build a strategic plan AND upgrade their Business Operating System (BOS) so the plan actually gets executed. OASYS is OneAccord's branded BOS, built on the Ninety OS model and run on the ninety.io software platform. Doug Hall presents the training videos and helped launch the practice; he has coached business operating systems since 2016 (first EOS-certified implementer in Washington State in 2017, later Pinnacle Business Guides and Scaling Up), and takes an independent, best-of-breed approach. Jesse Kreun is acting Managing Principal and leads the OASYS practice; questions about the practice go to Jesse. A CSP and OASYS are independent offerings: every engagement starts with some form of fact-finding assessment, which is not always a full CSP; a CSP usually recommends OASYS, and OASYS can begin without a CSP. Three owner objectives: (1) achieve the business purpose and goals (mission, vision, values, legacy, aligned team); (2) increase the owner's time freedom by building a self-managing company with a strong leadership team; (3) optimize enterprise value, mainly by reducing owner dependence and improving financial performance, which opens exit options including a financial exit or an operating exit (e.g. CEO emeritus). If an owner is comfortable on all three, they won't buy; there must be pain in at least one, or a vague dissatisfaction, a desire to be a 'category of one', or a sense the owner can't take the company to the next level alone (humility and hunger). Common strategic planning failures: no clear direction, misaligned teams, poor follow-through, 'shelfware' plans that never get executed (the execution gap), firefighting, bias, complexity. Strategic planning answers: where are we now, where do we want to be, how do we get there. Building blocks: vision, mission, core values, SWOT, long-term objectives, 90-day priorities ('Rocks'), KPIs, action plans, accountability structure. The practice is horizontal (no industry expertise needed), hired by the CEO, and works with the leadership team (the CEO's strategic direct reports). Engagement: onboarding and initial implementation, then a strategic plan refresh every 90 days anchored by an annual 2-day off-site retreat, typically as an annual plan of work billed as a monthly retainer. Do not quote prices; a managing principal guides pricing. It is a top-down upgrade that can cross-sell into functional work (marketing, sales, operations, interim/fractional leaders) and vice versa; OneAccord refers out legal and some CFO work. Every company that makes payroll already has a BOS: its current way of leading and managing (often informal, like a fish not knowing it's in water), shaped by the founder, shiny objects the CEO brings back from peer groups, and new managers' habits. Typical informal BOS tools: occasional off-site planning, a maybe-written strategic plan, a budget, monthly financials, weekly staff meetings, one-on-ones, all-hands, annual performance reviews. Upgrading means getting uncomfortable before getting comfortable again, so change management matters. Costs of an informal BOS: chaos, wasted time, inconsistent results, stalled growth, over-reliance on individuals, reduced company value. Deming: every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets. Owners can upgrade functions (marketing, sales, ops, finance) or upgrade the BOS and leadership team; prospects for OASYS usually find the leadership team has become the limiting factor. BOS lineage: Gerber (E-Myth), Jack Stack (Great Game of Business), Andy Grove and John Doerr (OKRs), Verne Harnish (Rockefeller Habits, Scaling Up), Gino Wickman (EOS/Traction), Franklin Covey (4 Disciplines of Execution), plus Lencioni and Collins; Ninety OS is the first software-based BOS and covers the best of EOS, 4DX, OKRs and parts of Scaling Up. Foundational tools: one-page strategic plan (core values, purpose, 10-year, 3-year, 1-year goals, 90-day Rocks), org chart with functional accountability, KPI scorecards with lead and lag measures, weekly team meetings with a set agenda, quarterly planning cadence. Ninety OS has 9 core competencies (vision, customer, goals, people, structure, data, meetings, process, enterprise value), continuously improved by working the system. ninety.io holds vision and planning, scorecard, Rocks, issues, meeting rhythms, people tools, processes, to-dos. Client options: do-it-yourself alone (read Traction), DIY with group coaching, or done-for-you implementer coaching (OneAccord's recommended full engagement). The coach is like a sports coach on the sidelines: not better at the game, better at watching and coaching. OneAccord always recommends the full coached engagement but can help budget-limited clients self-implement on ninety.io and stay their go-to resource. Success = steady improvement on ten factors (solid strategy, shared vision, right people in right seats, teamwork, right numbers/KPIs, consistent execution, solving issues / self-managing team, getting the right stuff done in 90-day focus, financial performance, enterprise value), not a single end goal. Process: baseline benchmarks (OneAccord business assessment, enterprise value appraisal, behavioral assessments such as DISC or Predictive Index, team tools such as Working Genius and Five Dysfunctions trust-building) -> situation analysis and proposal -> agreement with owner/CEO -> implementation workshops (foundations, goals, vision; full days or several half days, virtual or in person) -> coach the weekly team meetings and roll the agenda down -> schedule quarterly planning dates for a rolling 12 months -> facilitate 90-day off-sites (ideally in person) -> the first two-day session IS year one's annual session and carries the Foundation work -> three one-day quarterlies plus one two-day annual every year, ongoing with no planned end -> 'graduate' is allowed if the client can sustain the cadence itself, but it is not the design goal. This is the capstone exercise of the overview course. Grade generously on wording but strictly on substance: the learner should sound like a credible, consultative OneAccord principal.

blocks.promptHtml:
Different conditions: this prospect has already decided, and he's read the book.

The owner of a $15M electrical contractor says: “I've read Traction twice. I don't need a consultant in my business — I just want the software and someone to call when I get stuck. Can you do that, or not?”

What do you say?
rubric: Answers the question honestly and directly — yes, that's possible — rather than deflecting into a pitch
Names what the coached engagement adds that self-implementation doesn't: facilitated sessions, a cadence held by someone else, and a coach who sees what the team can't see about itself
Uses the coaching comparison without condescension — a coach isn't better at the game, better at watching it
Describes the self-implement path accurately (set up on ninety.io, we stay his resource) while still making the full engagement the recommendation
Quotes no price, routes cost and scope to the Managing Principal, and leaves with a concrete next step
blocks.coachContext: The client options are: do it alone (read Traction or Scaling Up); do it with group coaching; or done for you with an implementer coach, which OneAccord always recommends. For prospects who can't support a full engagement yet, we can set them up on ninety.io to self-implement and stay their go-to resource when bigger issues come up. The coach is like a sports coach on the sidelines: not better at the game than the players, better at watching, knowing what to look for and helping them improve. An owner who has read Traction twice is not a blank slate — respect what he knows and don't re-teach him the book. Success is steady improvement across ten factors (solid strategy, shared vision, right people in right seats, teamwork, right KPIs, consistent execution, a leadership team that solves its own issues, the right things done each 90 days, financial performance, enterprise value), not a single end goal. Do not quote prices; price and scope go to the Managing Principal.

blocks.label: Draft a real first year
blocks.instructions:
Take one prospect or client you'd genuinely recommend OASYS to, and draft the shape of their first year — the cadence, not the fees:
  1. The two-day onboarding: day one Foundation Setting, day two Vision and Goal Setting.
  2. The weekly rhythm: who's in the room, and what the agenda would be.
  3. Three quarterly sessions: roughly when, across twelve months.
  4. Year two and beyond: what their calendar looks like every year after this one.

Then mark the two things you'd have to confirm with the Managing Principal before promising anything — dates and cost are almost certainly two of them.
